title: Basque to the future: Andoni Iraola fired up for first Merseyside derby
summary: Liverpool head coach sees parallels with Athletic v Sociedad derby as he comes up against his old foe David Moyes “I haven’t lived this derby,” Andoni Iraola acknowledged, and yet he already feels it. A former Athletic Bilbao captain coming up against an ex-Real Sociedad head coach needs no instruction on the importance of winning a derby, whether in the Basque country or on Merseyside. But this week, as the Liverpool head coach approaches his first experience of the latter, there has been no escape. “It has been very easy for me here,” says Iraola of his five months on Merseyside. “Family-wise we have settled in really well. People here are very friendly, they love to talk to you but in a very respectful way. This week there has been a lot [of interaction with Liverpool fans], especially with playing big games against United and Everton. ‘We need to win, we need to win,’ they say.” Continue reading...

title: The Renéessance is over but Arsenal’s chaotic cycle will go on without further change | Suzanne Wrack
summary: Renée Slegers’ exit, 18 months on from European glory, was inevitable but much of the blame lies with those higher up The Renéessance is over. Three down, how many more to go? The exit of Arsenal manager, Renée Slegers, 18 months after delivering European glory was somewhat inevitable, her position made untenable after six home draws in six games and just 15 points from 11 games, but will it solve the Gunners’ problems? There were high expectations in north London prior to the season, after difficult starts in back-to-back WSL campaigns put them outside a real title challenge within the opening few games. title: Aaron Rodgers texts into Amazon broadcast to defend himself as Steelers beat Broncos
summary: Denver Broncos 5-27 Pittsburgh Steelers Quarterback was released after blasting own coach At the end of a chaotic week that saw Aaron Rodgers’ highly public departure from Pittsburgh thanks to a rift with head coach Mike McCarthy – a turn of events that former coach Mike Tomlin called a “dumpster fire” and threatened to turn one of the league’s most stable franchises into a punchline – it felt on some level like The Steeler Way was at stake on Friday. Those Steelers left to navigate the fallout responded with a dominant 27-5 victory over the Denver Broncos that will turn down the volume, at least for a week. Continue reading...

title: Brit-splaining Botham and the impossible task of defining a sporting life without limits | Will Woodward
summary: Explaining the England all-rounder and now great-grandfather reveals a career that refuses to fit in a single box Across the Guardian sportsdesk this week it emerged that a young American colleague didn’t know who Ian Botham was. And why should she? She is young and American. And so the rest of us Brit-splained in five sentences, rehearsed here – and edited to make us sound better than we actually did. Botham is comfortably among the top five most famous living British sportspeople, certainly among those of a certain age. In 1981 he won (almost) single‑handed (arguably) the greatest Ashes series by bending it to his will. He was on the front pages as well as back in the 1980s, for soft drugs, suspensions and shagging. He is a member of the House of Lords. He is the most English of sports stars, Australians love him, and his grandson James plays rugby union for Wales, which is why we started talking about him. title: South Africa have pushed the limits of rugby – time to show they still have the edge
summary: Rassie Erasmus has forged an iron bond in his squad but France could push them to breaking point at Twickenham At its best, Test rugby is a game played right out on the edge, where the players push the very limits of what anyone ought to be capable of. Out there the sport sells itself. In those moments it doesn’t matter if you know what a 50-22 is, or whether that was a hip-drop tackle or not, and no one needs a new Hemisphere Shield, or another message on the big screen telling everyone in the stadium to “Make Some Noise!” When it reaches that pitch of incomparable intensity, emotion and endeavour, Test rugby demands your attention whether you know it all or nothing at all. Stretches of this Nations Championship have been played out there, on the farthest reaches of the sport. Wales lived there for 80 minutes in their 35-28 win over the All Blacks a fortnight ago and were rewarded with one of the most famous results in their history. England came closer to it than they had been in a very long time during their own record 37-12 victory against New Zealand a week later. France got there when they were clinging on to their two-point win against South Africa in Paris, so did Ireland in the closing moments in Dublin days later, when they beat the Springboks by three and all the talk of a backlash be damned.
